sections.title: The recursive gradient descent sequence
sections.intro: The convergence argument is first proved for an arbitrary scalar gap sequence. This keeps the finite induction, scalar limits, and norm-limit argument separate from strong convexity and smoothness. Write $x_n=\lean{iterate}\,g\,\alpha\,x_0\,n$.

blocks.title: Imports used by the rate argument
blocks.explanation: The first import provides real normed spaces and their subtraction and scalar multiplication. The next two provide continuous square roots and the limit $\rho^n\to0$ for $0\le\rho<1$. The final three import tactics for clearing denominators, proving positivity, and checking polynomial identities. Imports provide proved library lemmas and tactic implementations; they do not add hypotheses to the theorems below.

blocks.title: Namespace, filters, and normed-space hypotheses
blocks.explanation: \lean{namespace GradientDescent} puts the declarations under a common prefix. \lean{open Filter} makes filter terminology such as \lean{atTop} available, while the topology scope enables neighborhood notation. The braces around $H$ declare an implicit type parameter. Square brackets request instances of a normed additive commutative group and a real normed vector space. These supply $x-y$, $\norm{x}$, and $\alpha\mathbin{\bullet}x$. No completeness or inner product is needed for this file.

blocks.title: Definition by recursion on the natural number
blocks.explanation:
The result type $\N\to H$ says that the definition returns a sequence. The two pattern-matching clauses implement exactly
\[
x_0=x_0,\qquad x_{n+1}=x_n-\alpha g(x_n).
\]
Here the $x_0$ on the right is the supplied starting point; the left denotes the zeroth sequence term. In Lean, \lean{*} is real multiplication and the bullet in the code is scalar multiplication of a vector. The recursive calls use $n$ rather than $n+1$, so Lean accepts the definition as terminating structural recursion.

blocks.title: The zeroth term is a simplification rule
blocks.explanation: \lean{rfl} proves equality by definitional reduction: unfolding the zero clause of \lean{iterate} makes both sides the same expression. The attribute \lean{@[simp]} registers this identity with the simplifier. Later, \lean{simpa only [iterate_zero]} replaces the initial iterate by the supplied $x_0$ in a rate bound.

blocks.title: The successor term is a simplification rule
blocks.explanation:
This is the successor clause of the definition, again proved by \lean{rfl}. For every $n$,
\[
\lean{iterate}\,g\,\alpha\,x_0\,(n+1)=x_n-\alpha g(x_n).
\]
Its simplification attribute makes the recursion available to proofs. In the main convergence theorem, \lean{rw [iterate_succ]} rewrites the left side of a one-step gap statement into precisely the gradient-step expression already controlled by the descent theorem.

sections.title: Induction gives the geometric scalar bound
sections.intro: For the finite estimate, the only sign assumption is $\rho\ge0$. The terms $a_n$ themselves need not be nonnegative. Assume $a_{n+1}\le\rho a_n$; induction proves $a_n\le\rho^n a_0$.

blocks.title: State the induction problem
blocks.explanation:
The implicit parameter \lean{a} is a real sequence. The hypothesis \lean{hstep} has type $\forall n,\ a_{n+1}\le\rho a_n$, and the explicit argument $n$ selects the desired term. The goal following the colon is
\[
a_n\le\rho^n a_0.
\]
The statement deliberately does not require $\rho<1$: that restriction is needed only when taking a limit.

blocks.title: Base case and induction hypothesis
blocks.explanation: \lean{induction n with} splits the proof into zero and successor cases. At zero, \lean{simp} evaluates $\rho^0=1$ and $1a_0=a_0$, leaving the reflexive inequality $a_0\le a_0$. In the successor branch, \lean{ih} is the induction hypothesis $a_n\le\rho^n a_0$; the remaining goal is $a_{n+1}\le\rho^{n+1}a_0$.

blocks.title: Three links of the induction calculation
blocks.explanation:
The \lean{calc} block proves a chain whose intermediate inequalities compose by transitivity:
\[
a_{n+1}\le\rho a_n\le\rho(\rho^n a_0)=\rho^{n+1}a_0.
\]
The first link is \lean{hstep n}. The second uses \lean{mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left}: multiplying the induction hypothesis on the left preserves order because the supplied hypothesis proves $\rho\ge0$. No assumption about the sign of $a_0$ is needed. The last link is an equality: \lean{rw [pow_succ]} expands $\rho^{n+1}=\rho^n\rho$, and \lean{ring} checks associativity and commutativity of real multiplication.

sections.title: The objective gap is an instance of the scalar bound
sections.intro: Let $\Delta_n=f(x_n)-f(z)$. The previous theorem applies directly to this real sequence. In this statement, $H$ can be any type, because evaluating $f$ does not require vector operations.

blocks.title: Omit unused typeclasses and specialize the sequence
blocks.explanation:
\lean{omit} removes both previously declared normed-space instances from this theorem's context. Its assumptions are just $\rho\ge0$ and $\Delta_{n+1}\le\rho\Delta_n$; its conclusion is
\[
\Delta_n\le\rho^n\Delta_0.
\]
The proof is a direct theorem application. The named argument \lean{a := fun n => f (x n) - f z} explicitly chooses the sequence $a_n=\Delta_n$; \lean{fun} constructs a function. The remaining arguments provide the sign proof, the step proof, and the term index. Lean checks that the specialized conclusion is exactly the displayed goal. There is no omitted proof obligation.

sections.title: The geometrically bounded gap tends to zero
sections.intro: Now impose $0\le\rho<1$ and $\Delta_n\ge0$. The geometric upper envelope tends to zero, and the squeeze theorem transfers that limit to the gap.

blocks.title: State the filter limit and its sign hypotheses
blocks.explanation:
Both normed-space instances are again omitted: this is a scalar argument on values of $f$. Besides the step inequality, the theorem has separate hypotheses $0\le\rho$, $\rho<1$, and $0\le\Delta_n$ for every $n$. The expression \lean{Tendsto} with \lean{atTop} as source and the neighborhood filter of zero as target states the usual limit
\[
\Delta_n\longrightarrow0\quad(n\to\infty).
\]
The lower sign condition is now essential for the squeeze argument, even though it was unnecessary for the finite induction bound.

blocks.title: Prove that the geometric upper envelope tends to zero
blocks.explanation:
\lean{have hpow : ... := by} creates a named local proof with the displayed limit as its goal. The library theorem \lean{tendsto_pow_atTop_nhds_zero_of_lt_one} gives $\rho^n\to0$ from the two supplied sign and strict-bound hypotheses. Dot notation \lean{.mul_const} multiplies that convergent sequence by the fixed real number $\Delta_0$, so
\[
\rho^n\Delta_0\longrightarrow0\cdot\Delta_0=0.
\]
\lean{simpa} simplifies the limiting product to zero and checks that the resulting statement matches \lean{hpow}.

blocks.title: Close the limit by squeezing between zero and the envelope
blocks.explanation:
\lean{squeeze_zero} receives three proofs, in order: the lower inequality $0\le\Delta_n$, the upper inequality $\Delta_n\le\rho^n\Delta_0$, and the upper envelope's limit. The second argument is the geometric-gap theorem with its index left as a function argument. Thus the exact mathematical sandwich is
\[
0\le\Delta_n\le\rho^n\Delta_0\longrightarrow0.
\]
\lean{exact} supplies the resulting proof of the target limit without further simplification.

sections.title: Convert the gap rate into a squared-distance rate
sections.intro: Suppose $m>0$ and $\frac m2\norm{x_n-z}^2\le\Delta_n$. Combine that lower bound with the geometric upper bound and divide by the positive number $m/2$.

blocks.title: State the lower bound and the requested distance bound
blocks.explanation:
Here \lean{omit} drops the real vector-space instance but keeps the normed additive group instance: subtraction and norm are used, whereas scalar multiplication of vectors is not. The real parameters have proofs $m>0$ and $\rho\ge0$. The hypotheses \lean{hlower} and \lean{hstep} hold for every $n$. The goal is the explicit estimate
\[
\norm{x_n-z}^2\le\frac2m\bigl(\rho^n\Delta_0\bigr).
\]
Only a finite estimate is claimed, so no hypothesis $\rho<1$ is present.

blocks.title: Chain the bounds and divide without reversing order
blocks.explanation:
The method \lean{.trans} combines two inequalities sharing their middle expression, producing
\[
\frac m2\norm{x_n-z}^2\le\Delta_n\le\rho^n\Delta_0.
\]
The local proof \lean{hdiv} then has goal $\norm{x_n-z}^2\le(\rho^n\Delta_0)/(m/2)$. The theorem \lean{le_div_iff}${}_0$ for a positive denominator says $A\le B/c$ if and only if $Ac\le B$ when $c>0$. Its \lean{.2} direction transforms the product inequality into the quotient inequality. \lean{positivity} derives $m/2>0$ from $m>0$, and \lean{simpa [mul_comm]} rearranges $(m/2)A$ into $A(m/2)$. Because the divisor is positive, the inequality direction is preserved.

blocks.title: Identify the quotient with the stated prefactor
blocks.explanation:
\lean{convert hdiv using 1} uses the proved quotient inequality while leaving equality of the two right-hand expressions as the remaining goal. \lean{field_simp} clears their denominators and verifies
\[
\frac{\rho^n\Delta_0}{m/2}=\frac2m\bigl(\rho^n\Delta_0\bigr).
\]
This step changes only the algebraic presentation of the bound; the order argument has already been completed using $m/2>0$.

sections.title: Squared-distance decay implies convergence of the iterates
sections.intro: The generic sequence theorem uses only a normed additive group. It squeezes the squared norms to zero, uses continuity of square root, and then applies the distance characterization of convergence.

blocks.title: The norm-convergence theorem and its assumptions
blocks.explanation: The vector-space instance is omitted as above. The target \lean{Tendsto x atTop} to the neighborhood filter of $z$ means $x_n\to z$ in the norm topology. The proof assumes $m>0$, $0\le\rho<1$, the quadratic gap lower bound, and the gap step inequality. It does not separately assume nonnegative gaps: their lower bound already implies that sign. No completeness of $H$ is required because a candidate limit $z$ is supplied.

blocks.title: The full distance envelope tends to zero
blocks.explanation:
The geometric power theorem first yields $\rho^n\to0$. The method \lean{.mul_const} multiplies on the right by $\Delta_0$, then \lean{.const_mul} multiplies on the left by the fixed number $2/m$. Consequently
\[
\frac2m\bigl(\rho^n\Delta_0\bigr)\longrightarrow\frac2m(0\cdot\Delta_0)=0.
\]
The final \lean{simpa} simplifies this limiting scalar expression and produces the local proof \lean{hbound}.

blocks.title: Squeeze the squared norm itself
blocks.explanation:
The new local goal is $\norm{x_n-z}^2\to0$. For each $n$, \lean{sq_nonneg} proves the lower inequality; underscores let Lean infer the squared real number. The previously established distance theorem supplies the upper inequality, while \lean{hbound} supplies its limit:
\[
0\le\norm{x_n-z}^2\le\frac2m\bigl(\rho^n\Delta_0\bigr)\longrightarrow0.
\]
These are exactly the three inputs to \lean{squeeze_zero}, yielding \lean{hsq}.

blocks.title: Take square roots and recover convergence in the space
blocks.explanation:
The method \lean{hsq.sqrt} uses continuity of the real square-root function, including at zero. It initially proves $\sqrt{\norm{x_n-z}^2}\to\sqrt0$. The norm is nonnegative, so \lean{Real.sqrt_sq (norm_nonneg _)} rewrites the left side to $\norm{x_n-z}$; \lean{Real.sqrt_zero} rewrites the limit to zero. Thus
\[
\norm{x_n-z}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Finally, \lean{dist_eq_norm} identifies $\operatorname{dist}(x_n,z)$ with this norm. The \lean{.2} direction of \lean{tendsto_iff_dist_tendsto_zero} converts distance tending to zero into $x_n\to z$, closing the theorem.

sections.title: The rate and the admissible step-size interval
sections.intro:
Return to the complete real Hilbert space and put
\[
q=1-m\alpha(2-L\alpha),\qquad\rho=\max\{0,q\}.
\]
The maximum ensures a nonnegative scalar rate even in a one-point space, where the hypotheses need not force $m\le L$. The step restriction $0<\alpha<2/L$ ensures $\rho<1$.

blocks.title: Dependencies of the final convergence theorem
blocks.explanation: The three imports provide the minimizer theorem, the smooth quadratic upper bound, and the generic iteration and rate results just proved. The local linter option only disables a source-file copyright-header style check; it has no mathematical effect and supplies no theorem or hypothesis.

blocks.title: The complete real Hilbert-space setting
blocks.explanation: The nonnegative-real scope enables the type $\R_{\ge0}$ for $L$; coercion of $L$ to $\R$ is explicit in the source. The \lean{noncomputable section} permits the classical definitions involved in the gradient and minimizer argument. The namespace and filter scopes supply the familiar declaration and limit notation. The three typeclasses state that $H$ is a normed additive group with a real inner product and is complete. Thus this theorem works in arbitrary complete real Hilbert spaces, without a finite-dimensional assumption.

blocks.title: Define the clamped rate and prove its lower sign
blocks.explanation: The function \lean{rate} returns the real scalar $\rho=\max\{0,1-m\alpha(2-L\alpha)\}$. The theorem \lean{rate_nonneg} applies \lean{le_max_left}, the elementary inequality $a\le\max(a,b)$, with $a=0$. This proves $0\le\rho$ for every choice of parameters. The statement uses no positivity assumptions, because taking the maximum itself establishes the sign. In a one-point Hilbert space every gap and distance is zero, so allowing such parameters causes no difficulty for later rate bounds.

blocks.title: State the strict upper bound on the rate
blocks.explanation: The parameters are implicit, while the four explicit proofs assert $m>0$, $L>0$, $\alpha>0$, and $\alpha<2/L$. The goal is $\rho<1$. The separate proof of $L>0$ matters when converting the quotient step-size condition into a product condition.

blocks.title: Use positivity to show both entries of the maximum are below one
blocks.explanation:
The \lean{.mp} direction of the positive-denominator theorem \lean{lt_div_iff}${}_0$ gives $\alpha L<2$ from $\alpha<2/L$. Hence $2-L\alpha>0$. The first \lean{mul_pos} proves $m\alpha>0$ using $m>0$ and $\alpha>0$; its outer application reduces the remaining local goal to positivity of $2-L\alpha$, which \lean{nlinarith} obtains from $\alpha L<2$. Therefore
\[
m\alpha(2-L\alpha)>0,\qquad q=1-m\alpha(2-L\alpha)<1.
\]
\lean{max_lt} asks for both $0<1$ and $q<1$. \lean{norm_num} proves the numeric inequality; \lean{linarith} derives the second from the positive product. The result is $\rho<1$.

sections.title: When the clamping disappears
sections.intro: If $m\le L$, the raw scalar factor $q$ is already nonnegative. The following auxiliary theorem proves the familiar formula $\rho=q$ directly. This auxiliary comparison assumption is not required by the main convergence theorem.

blocks.title: The equality to be proved
blocks.explanation:
The hypotheses are $m\le L$, $L>0$, $\alpha>0$, and $\alpha<2/L$. The target identifies the defined maximum with its second argument:
\[
\max\{0,1-m\alpha(2-L\alpha)\}=1-m\alpha(2-L\alpha).
\]
To apply the corresponding maximum identity it suffices to prove $0\le1-m\alpha(2-L\alpha)$.

blocks.title: Find a nonnegative common multiplier
blocks.explanation:
As before, division by the positive $L$ gives $\alpha L<2$. Consequently $2-L\alpha>0$, and \lean{mul_nonneg}, supplied with the weak sign $\alpha\ge0$, reduces the local product-sign goal to that second factor. \lean{nlinarith} closes it from the product step-size inequality. Thus
\[
0\le\alpha(2-L\alpha).
\]
The conversion from a strict sign to a weak sign is encoded by the proof method \lean{.le}.

blocks.title: Bound the raw product by one using a square
blocks.explanation:
Multiplying $m\le L$ on the right by the nonnegative common factor preserves order:
\[
m\alpha(2-L\alpha)\le L\alpha(2-L\alpha).
\]
The explicit \lean{sq_nonneg} input gives $(L\alpha-1)^2\ge0$. Expanding it yields
\[
L\alpha(2-L\alpha)=1-(L\alpha-1)^2\le1.
\]
\lean{nlinarith} verifies this polynomial consequence, recording it as \lean{hbound}.

blocks.title: Finish the maximum identity
blocks.explanation: \lean{apply max_eq_right} changes the target equality into the remaining inequality $0\le q$. The two product bounds just obtained imply $m\alpha(2-L\alpha)\le1$, hence $0\le1-m\alpha(2-L\alpha)$. \lean{nlinarith} closes this goal by rearranging those inequalities. Therefore the clamp is unnecessary whenever $m\le L$.

sections.title: Smoothness gives the descent estimate
sections.intro:
Set $G=\nabla f(x)$ and $x^+=x-\alpha G$. Substituting this step into the quadratic upper bound gives
\[
f(x^+)\le f(x)-\alpha\left(1-\frac{L\alpha}{2}\right)\norm{G}^2.
\]
This inequality is algebraically valid for every real $\alpha$; its coefficient becomes positive when the admissible step-size assumptions are later used.

blocks.title: The one-step objective decrease statement
blocks.explanation: The two function hypotheses are real differentiability and the Lipschitz bound on \lean{gradient f}. The point $x$ and real scalar $\alpha$ are arbitrary. The displayed target is the descent inequality above. No sign or upper bound on $\alpha$ appears in this lemma, so it proves the substitution identity and upper estimate independently of step-size admissibility.

blocks.title: Substitute the step and simplify the inner product and norm
blocks.explanation:
The smoothness theorem is applied with $y=x-\alpha G$, producing
\[
f(x^+)\le f(x)+\ip{G}{x^+-x}+ rac L2
orm{x^+-x}^2.
\]
\lean{rw ... at h} rewrites the local inequality rather than the main goal. The first rewrite gives $x^+-x=-\alpha G$. Inner-product linearity then gives $\ip{G}{-\alpha G}=-\alpha\ip{G}{G}=-\alpha
orm{G}^2$. The norm rewrites remove the negation and use $
orm{\alpha G}=|\alpha|
orm{G}$. At this stage the remaining quadratic term is $ rac L2(|\alpha|
orm{G})^2$.

blocks.title: Expand the squared norm and collect the coefficient
blocks.explanation:
\lean{mul_pow} expands $(|\alpha|
orm{G})^2$ as $|\alpha|^2
orm{G}^2$, and \lean{sq_abs} replaces $|\alpha|^2$ by $\alpha^2$. Thus the local inequality becomes
\[
f(x^+)\le f(x)-\alpha
orm{G}^2+ rac L2\alpha^2
orm{G}^2.
\]
\lean{nlinarith} checks that this right-hand side equals $f(x)-\alpha(1-L\alpha/2)
orm{G}^2$ and concludes the requested inequality. The tactic supplies polynomial rearrangement here, rather than a new analytic estimate.

sections.title: Combine descent and the gradient lower bound to contract the gap
sections.intro: Let $z$ be stationary and set $\Delta=f(x)-f(z)$. Strong convexity gives $2m\Delta\le\norm{\nabla f(x)}^2$ and $\Delta\ge0$. With the positive descent coefficient $c=\alpha(1-L\alpha/2)$, this yields the raw gap factor $q$; nonnegativity of $\Delta$ then allows replacement of $q$ by $\rho=\max\{0,q\}$.

blocks.title: All hypotheses for a single contracted step
blocks.explanation:
The function is differentiable, $m$-strongly convex on the whole space, and has an $L$-Lipschitz gradient. The signs are $m>0$, $L>0$, $\alpha>0$, and $\alpha<2/L$. The reference point $z$ is implicit, and \lean{hz} supplies stationarity $\nabla f(z)=0$. The goal is
\[
f(x-\alpha\nabla f(x))-f(z)\le\rho\bigl(f(x)-f(z)\bigr).
\]
This lemma assumes a stationary point; the main theorem later constructs one, rather than adding its existence to the user-facing hypotheses.

blocks.title: Prove the descent coefficient is nonnegative
blocks.explanation:
Since $L>0$, the step condition gives $\alpha L<2$. It follows that $1-L\alpha/2>0$. \lean{mul_nonneg} uses $\alpha\ge0$ and reduces the local goal to nonnegativity of the second factor; \lean{nlinarith} derives that factor's sign. The resulting proof \lean{hc} states
\[
0\le c=\alpha(1-L\alpha/2).
\]
This sign must be established before multiplying the gradient lower bound by $c$, because multiplication by a negative number would reverse order.

blocks.title: Turn the upper-gap inequality into a lower bound for gradient norm
Prove nonnegative gap before changing the rate
blocks.explanation:
Stationarity allows \lean{strong_lower_gap} to give
\[
\frac m2\norm{x-z}^2\le\Delta.
\]
\lean{positivity} proves that its left side is nonnegative using $m>0$ and nonnegativity of a square. \lean{linarith} combines these two inequalities to get $0\le\Delta$. This separate fact is used in the last line when replacing the raw factor $q$ by its nonnegative clamp.

blocks.title: Derive the raw factor, then use the maximum safely
blocks.explanation:
The inequalities recorded as \lean{hscaled} and \lean{hdesc} give
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(x^+)-f(z)&\le\Delta-c\norm{\nabla f(x)}^2\\
&\le\Delta-2mc\Delta\\
&=\bigl(1-m\alpha(2-L\alpha)\bigr)\Delta=q\Delta.
\end{aligned}
\]
\lean{nlinarith} verifies this combination and the identity $2mc=m\alpha(2-L\alpha)$. The theorem \lean{le_max_right} proves $q\le\max(0,q)=\rho$. Multiplying this inequality on the right by the proven $\Delta\ge0$ preserves order, so $q\Delta\le\rho\Delta$. Finally \lean{hraw.trans} composes the two bounds. If $q<0$, the raw inequality and nonnegativity of both the current and next gaps force the compatible zero-gap behavior (the next gap is nonnegative by \lean{strong_lower_gap} at $x^+$); the clamp still yields a valid estimate.

sections.title: Assemble existence, uniqueness, limits, and quantitative bounds
sections.intro: This final theorem supplies a single point $z$ satisfying all conclusions. Its proof first obtains the stationary minimizer, then applies the generic rate lemmas to the concrete recursive gradient descent sequence. Write $x_n=\lean{iterate}\,(\lean{gradient}\,f)\,\alpha\,x_0\,n$ and $\Delta_n=f(x_n)-f(z)$.

blocks.title: The full list of input hypotheses
blocks.explanation:
The implicit function $f:H\to\R$, scalars $m,\alpha\in\R$, and $L\in\R_{\ge0}$ are followed by explicit proof arguments. \lean{hdiff} supplies differentiability; \lean{hsc} supplies $\lean{StrongConvexOn}$ on the whole space with parameter $m$; \lean{hLip} supplies $L$-Lipschitz continuity of the gradient. The remaining proof arguments assert
\[
m>0,\quad L>0,\quad\alpha>0,\quad\alpha<2/L.
\]
The starting point $x_0:H$ is unrestricted. There is no minimizer or stationary-point hypothesis here. The complete Hilbert-space typeclasses declared earlier are implicit assumptions on $H$.

blocks.title: Existential minimizer and both limits
blocks.explanation: The existential quantifier requests one $z:H$ with a chain of conjunctions. Their first five components state: $\nabla f(z)=0$; $f(z)\le f(x)$ for every $x$; every other global minimizer $y$ equals $z$; $x_n\to z$; and $f(x_n)\to f(z)$. The conjunctions are right-associated, so a tuple can later supply these proofs in this exact order. The \lean{Tendsto} statements encode limits as $n$ tends to infinity through the natural numbers. All components refer to the same existential witness.

blocks.title: The per-iteration quantitative conclusions
blocks.explanation:
The final component universally quantifies over $n\in\N$ and asks for three more conjuncts:
\[
\begin{gathered}
0\le\Delta_n,\qquad\Delta_n\le\rho^n\Delta_0,\\
\norm{x_n-z}^2\le\frac2m\bigl(\rho^n\Delta_0\bigr),\qquad
\Delta_0=f(x_0)-f(z),\quad\rho=\lean{rate}\,m\,\alpha\,L.
\end{gathered}
\]
The exponent is a natural-number power. The displayed prefactor $2/m$ is meaningful because $m>0$. The terminating \lean{:= by} begins the proof of the entire existential statement, not just the final bound.

blocks.title: Choose the stationary minimizer and prepare the generic hypotheses
blocks.explanation:
\lean{obtain} destructures an existential or conjunction into named local values and proofs. The first use obtains $z$ and $\nabla f(z)=0$ from \lean{exists_stationary}; the second obtains global minimality and uniqueness at that point. The next two lines record $0\le\rho$ and $\rho<1$ from the rate lemmas. Finally \lean{have hlower (n : ...)} creates a family of proofs
\[
\frac m2\norm{x_n-z}^2\le\Delta_n\quad\text{for every }n.
\]
The application of \lean{strong_lower_gap} uses the newly obtained stationarity proof. Thus all of the objects and signs required by the abstract rate theorems are now available.

blocks.title: Connect the recursive sequence to the one-step gap lemma
blocks.explanation:
The local goal is the family of inequalities $\Delta_{n+1}\le\rho\Delta_n$. \lean{rw [iterate_succ]} replaces $x_{n+1}$ by $x_n-\alpha\nabla f(x_n)$, leaving
\[
f(x_n-\alpha\nabla f(x_n))-f(z)\le\rho\bigl(f(x_n)-f(z)\bigr).
\]
This is precisely \lean{gradient_descent_gap_step} at $x=x_n$. \lean{exact} passes the differentiability, strong-convexity, Lipschitz, sign, step-size, and stationarity proofs in their declared order. The last underscore lets Lean infer the point $x_n$ from the current goal.

blocks.title: Obtain gap nonnegativity and the two generic limits
blocks.explanation: Global minimality gives $f(z)\le f(x_n)$; \lean{sub_nonneg.mpr} converts this into $0\le\Delta_n$. The underscore in \lean{hmin _} is inferred as $x_n$. The generic norm-convergence theorem applied to the concrete sequence then yields \lean{hx}, the proof $x_n\to z$. The scalar gap theorem yields \lean{hf}, the proof $\Delta_n\to0$. Their hypotheses are the lower bound and one-step inequality just proved, together with $m>0$ and $0\le\rho<1$.

blocks.title: Recover objective-value convergence and fill the existential tuple
blocks.explanation:
Adding the constant $f(z)$ to \lean{hf} proves $\Delta_n+f(z)\to0+f(z)$. The restricted simplifier rewrites the source using \lean{sub_add_cancel} and the target using \lean{zero_add}, yielding $f(x_n)\to f(z)$. The \lean{refine} tuple then supplies, in order, the witness $z$, stationarity, minimality, uniqueness, norm convergence, and objective convergence. Its final function \lean{fun n} supplies the universally quantified triple. The first entry of that triple is the already proved $0\le\Delta_n$; the two question-mark holes create only the remaining bound goals
\[
\Delta_n\le\rho^n\Delta_0,
\qquad\norm{x_n-z}^2\le\frac2m\bigl(\rho^n\Delta_0\bigr).
\]
These are ordinary intermediate proof goals, both discharged immediately below.

blocks.title: Close the objective-gap rate subgoal
blocks.explanation: The first bullet focuses the first remaining goal from \lean{refine}. The generic \lean{geometric_gap_bound} gives $\Delta_n\le\rho^n(f(x_{\mathrm{sequence},0})-f(z))$ for the chosen sequence. \lean{simpa only [iterate_zero]} evaluates that sequence's zeroth term as the supplied $x_0$. Hence its initial gap becomes exactly $f(x_0)-f(z)$ and the theorem matches the first target without any additional hypothesis.

blocks.title: Close the squared-distance rate subgoal
blocks.explanation:
The second bullet focuses the final remaining goal. The generic \lean{squared_distance_bound} uses $m>0$, $\rho\ge0$, \lean{hlower}, and \lean{hstep} to prove
\[
\norm{x_n-z}^2\le\frac2m\rho^n\bigl(f(x_{\mathrm{sequence},0})-f(z)\bigr).
\]
